facts.statement: Cathayornis yandica was a small bird with an elongated, toothy beak and feet adapted for perching.
facts.quote: Cathayornis yandica was a small enantiornithean with a slightly elongated, toothy snout and perching feet.

facts.statement: Like other Enantiornithes, Cathayornis possessed large claws on its first two wing fingers used for support.
facts.quote: Like most other Enantiornithes, it had large claws on the first two fingers that supported the wing.

facts.statement: Only one definitive fossil specimen, catalogued as IVPP V9769, is currently known for Cathayornis yandica.
facts.quote: According to most recent studies, only one specimen can be definitively assigned to this species, a fossil catalogued as number IVPP V9769 and currently housed in the collections of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.

facts.statement: Cathayornis is distinguished from similar birds like Sinornis by its larger size and a shorter, straighter first finger with a longer claw.
facts.quote: Cathayornis can be told apart from similar Enantiornithes (especially Sinornis, Eocathayornis, and Houornis) by its larger size, a shorter and straighter first finger with a slightly longer claw, and other anatomical details.

facts.statement: Cathayornis yandica was one of the first Enantiornithes species discovered in China.
facts.quote: It is known definitively from only one species, Cathayornis yandica, one of the first Enantiornithes found in China.

facts.statement: Several species previously assigned to Cathayornis have since been reclassified or deemed invalid.
facts.quote: Several additional species were once incorrectly classified as Cathayornis, and have since been reclassified or regarded as nomina dubia.

facts.statement: In 2002, Paul Sereno and colleagues classified Cathayornis as a junior synonym of Sinornis.
facts.quote: Paul Sereno et al., in 2002, considered Cathayornis a junior synonym of Sinornis.

facts.statement: Researchers questioned the validity of Cathayornis aberransis after finding its distinguishing features, such as a skull crest, were inaccurately described.
facts.quote: Jingmai O'Connor and Gareth Dyke (2010) found that many of the supposedly distinct features of C. aberransis (such as the base of a crest on the skull) had been inaccurately described, casting doubt on the few remaining features separating it from C. yandica, and suggested that further study was needed to determine its validity.

facts.statement: Cathayornis fossils come from the Jiufotang Formation in Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Cathayornis is a genus of enantiornithean birds, from the Jiufotang Formation of Liaoning, People's Republic of China.

facts.statement: Cathayornis lived during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: It is known definitively from only one species, Cathayornis yandica, one of the first Enantiornithes found in China.

facts.statement: Cathayornis inhabited the Early Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation in what is now Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Cathayornis es un género extinto de avialano perteneciente al clado Enantiornithes que habitó en el Cretácico inferior en lo que hoy es la Formación Jiufotang de Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: Cathayornis lived between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (121.4 to 113.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Cathayornis is classified within the subclass Enantiornithes.
The genus Cathayornis was described by Zhou, Jin, and Zhang in 1992.
Cathayornis yandica is the type species of the genus Cathayornis.

rejected.statement: O'Connor and Dyke (2010) debated that Cathayornis and Sinornis are distinct species, differing in wing claw proportions, digit structure, pelvis, and pygostyle size.
rejected.quote: O'Connor and Dyke concluded that despite the earlier opinion of Sereno and colleagues, the two birds were not synonyms and in fact differ in several clear ways, including different proportions in the wing claws and digits, differences in the pelvis, and size of the pygostyle.

rejected.statement: Wang and Liu (2015) moved Cathayornis caudatus to the new genus Houornis.
rejected.quote: Wang and Liu determined that C. caudatus could be differentiated from Cathayornis and placed it in the new genus Houornis.

rejected.statement: Wang and Liu (2015) considered Cathayornis chabuensis a nomen dubium.
rejected.quote: On the other hand, they considered C. chabuensis a nomen dubium.
